rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window, observe all 10 compounds, and identify critical pairs. The moderate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
Change only gradient duration to measure how the close early cluster responds to slope. This will distinguish gradient-responsive overlaps from pairs that need temperature-driven selectivity changes.
Test the high-temperature endpoint against injection 1 to probe selectivity in the early three-peak cluster. Higher temperature should also preserve the favorable last-peak time.

Keep the favorable high-temperature selectivity and use a shallower gradient to improve the sole unresolved pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving a chance to reach the maximum CRF.

The remaining close pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a higher starting organic fraction to alter its selectivity instead. Keep temperature at 60 C and monitor retention of the earliest peak.

Increase the starting organic fraction one more step, following the improvement in the critical pair from R 1.14 to 1.32. Other pairs retain resolution margin, and the last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.
The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a shorter gradient for faster fully resolved elution. Retain injection 6 as the benchmark if compression pushes any pair below R 1.5.

Narrow the gradient window to soften the slope between injections 6 and 7, aiming to restore both marginal pairs above R 1.5 while remaining faster than injection 6. The final organic fraction remains well above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Test whether another increase in starting organic fraction can shorten retention while preserving full resolution at the gentler 10-minute gradient. Watch the early cluster for compression; injection 8 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Compare directly with injection 8 to measure temperature sensitivity near the fastest fully resolved method. A modest temperature decrease may redistribute resolution within the early cluster and reveal whether further gradient compression is feasible.

Return to 60 C and test a slope between the fully resolved injection 8 and slightly compressed injection 7, seeking a shorter maximum-score method. The final organic fraction should still place the last peak near the end of the gradient rather than deep into the hold.
Injection 11 still has a pair below R 1.5 despite its rounded CRF of 1.000. Test a shallower gradient than injection 6 to build resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

With maximum-score methods secured, explore the low-temperature endpoint for an alternative elution order that might resolve the early cluster under a faster gradient. The broad final organic fraction limits the risk of missing late compounds.

Return to favorable high-temperature selectivity and lengthen injection 9's gradient to recover its sole deficient pair. This tests whether the higher starting organic fraction can provide a fully resolved alternative with greater resolution margin than injection 8.

Use the proven starting fraction and temperature with a shallower gradient to increase critical-pair resolution margin. Extrapolation from injections 6 and 12 places the last peak near 9 minutes, still within the maximum-score time window.

Slightly reduce the slope relative to injection 14 to lift its sole marginal pair above R 1.5. This should establish another maximum-score method while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Lower injection 11's endpoint one grid step to restore its marginal pair above R 1.5 while retaining a six-minute programmed gradient. The estimated last-peak elution fraction is about 0.62, so the endpoint should still be sufficient.

Test the remaining endpoint step between injections 7 and 8 to pinpoint the fastest fully resolved eight-minute gradient. The critical pair is near its threshold, so retain injection 8 if any resolution falls below 1.5.

Injection 18 confirms that further compression loses full resolution. Test one endpoint step below injection 8 to gain a little resolution margin with only a modest retention-time increase, while preserving the maximum CRF.

Test a slope between injection 14's marginal separation and injection 16's full resolution to find a faster maximum-score method at phi0 0.20. Injection 8 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method overall.

Match injection 8's successful gradient slope with a shorter programmed gradient, then test whether the final hold still elutes all compounds within 10 minutes. Early-cluster resolution should be preserved, but late-peak retention and resolution will determine whether this abbreviated gradient is useful.

Return to an endpoint that keeps the last peak inside the gradient and slightly soften injection 19's slope. This should preserve maximum CRF while improving the critical-pair margin, with less retention than injection 12.

Preserve injection 22's fully resolving slope while shortening the programmed gradient to six minutes. The last peak should elute near the gradient-to-hold transition, retaining maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Refine the resolution boundary at phi0 0.20 by testing the endpoint between injections 14 and 16. This should shorten injection 16 while potentially retaining full resolution; injection 8 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Use the final injection on a conservative refinement of injection 6, slightly reducing slope to preserve maximum CRF with additional resolution margin and a last peak expected below 7 minutes. Injection 8 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.
